content: 1. After soaking linens for 30 minutes, rinse them thoroughly with clean water. Then, hang the linens in a clean or dry area, preferably in direct sunlight, until they are completely dry. 2. Ensure proper waste management and disposal of personal protective equipment (PPE) and sharps in accordance with local regulations. a. Waste should be appropriately sorted and placed in designated bins at the point of use. b. Infectious, pathological, and sharps waste generated from the care of patients with suspected or confirmed Crimean-Congo Hemorrhagic Fever (CCHF) must follow national policies for minimizing, segregating, collecting, transporting, storing, treating, and disposing of waste. c. Regularly remove all waste from the patient-care environment to reduce the risk of microorganisms on healthcare waste contaminating clean items or being accidentally transmitted to staff and patients. 3. Patient care activities should be conducted in a clean and hygienic environment that supports infection prevention and control (IPC) practices. This includes ensuring the availability of water, sanitation, and hygiene (WASH) infrastructure and services, as well as appropriate IPC materials and equipment. 4. Health and care workers must be trained on standard and transmission-based precautions, including those specific to CCHF. They should also be trained in the use of standardized screening and triage algorithms to identify and isolate suspected and confirmed cases. 5. A protocol for assessing and managing occupational exposures among health and care workers should be in place. a. Occupational exposure is defined as any unprotected contact, including with non-intact skin, percutaneous or mucocutaneous exposure to blood, body fluids, secretions, or excretions from a suspected or confirmed CCHF patient, or unprotected exposure to contaminated equipment or surfaces during the performance of job duties. b. Health and care workers with identified exposure should: i. Be informed about the signs and symptoms of CCHF. ii. Self-monitor for signs and symptoms for 13 days after the last potential exposure. iii. Seek early medical care if symptoms develop. iv. Be excluded from work duties and undergo clinical assessment for diagnosis and management if they develop any signs or symptoms of infection. 6. Surveillance for healthcare-associated infections (HAIs) should be conducted. a. Health and care workers should monitor inpatients for signs and symptoms of CCHF. If a patient is suspected of developing CCHF during inpatient care, they should be immediately isolated with transmission-based precautions in place. b. Determine if the patient meets the case definition for suspected or confirmed CCHF according to local or WHO guidelines. 7. In the event of a healthcare-associated CCHF outbreak: a. A single case meeting the HAI case definition constitutes an outbreak. b. Cases should be isolated and managed according to operational guidelines. c. Conduct an investigation, including an audit of IPC practices, to identify potential sources of transmission. d. Dispose of all PPE and disposable patient care equipment as infectious waste. Ensure proper decontamination or reprocessing of all instruments and non-disposable equipment. 8. Contacts of suspected or confirmed CCHF cases should be identified and managed. a. Direct contacts are individuals who had direct physical exposure to a suspected or confirmed CCHF case without proper compliance with standard and transmission-based precautions. b. Indirect contacts are individuals potentially exposed to CCHF through shared environments or equipment used by a suspected or confirmed case. c. Contacts should be informed about the signs and symptoms of CCHF and monitored for 13 days after potential exposure. They should seek immediate medical care if symptoms develop. 9. In surgical and operating room settings, all personnel should use transmission-based precautions to prevent exposure to body fluids during procedures on suspected or confirmed CCHF patients. a. For aerosol-generating procedures, airborne and contact precautions with eye protection should be used. b. Perform terminal cleaning of the procedure room after the patient has left. Dispose of all PPE and disposable equipment as infectious waste, and ensure proper decontamination or reprocessing of all instruments and patient care equipment. 10. The World Health Organization (WHO) acknowledges the contributions of individuals and organizations involved in the development of this operational guide, including IPC experts, peer reviewers, and WHO staff from various regional offices.
